name: For Parents: Thinking For or Helping to Think
title: For Parents: Thinking For or Helping to Think
answer: This idea gives parents a way to tell whether AI at school is doing their child's thinking or helping the child think. The signs are usually visible at home, and the first step if they worry you is to talk with the teacher. The goal is not to keep AI away from children but to make sure the learning stays with them.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: Parents often ask whether AI at school is doing their child's thinking or helping the child think, and the ten patterns in the book make that question easier to answer. Most of the patterns, including drafting, logistics, language access, and early warning, involve adults using AI to do their own jobs better. Only a few patterns put AI directly in front of students, and those are the ones parents should watch. The idea solves a problem of visibility, because parents see the finished work at home but not always the process behind it. It gives them a simple way to judge what they are seeing.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The signs show up at home rather than only in the classroom. A child who can explain the homework in their own words, who revises after feedback, and who can do similar problems without a device is being helped to think. A child who turns in polished work but cannot explain it, or who panics when the tool is unavailable, may be leaning on AI to do the thinking. Figure 2.8 lists these signs side by side. If the signs worry a parent, the book says to start with the teacher, not the principal, and ask which tools the class uses, how they are set up, and whether there are regular checks without the tool.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure beyond Figure 2.8, or research finding for this idea. Figure 2.8 is described only as a side by side list of the signs, not as evidence from a study. This idea therefore rests on practice and observation rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The book is clear that the point is not to keep AI away from children, but to make sure it leaves the learning with them. Parents are told to bring concerns to the teacher first rather than the principal, and to ask about the tools, their setup, and whether regular checks happen without the tool. Most teachers welcome the question because they are watching for the same thing. The judgment about whether a child is being helped or is leaning on the tool stays with the parent and the teacher, not with the AI.
